opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a question I think about a lot, because it's very easy to fool yourself here. There's a version of this where everyone says, "I feel so much faster," and that feeling is real, but it doesn't automatically translate into the company getting more done. So I try to separate a few things.

The first level is the anecdotal, individual level. Engineers tell me they're using Claude to write a large fraction of their code, or that something that would have taken a week took an afternoon. I take that seriously, but I also know it's subject to bias. People notice the times the tool saved them and forget the times they spent an hour debugging something the model confidently got wrong.

The second level is task-level measurement: take a well-defined task, have people do it with and without the tools, and compare. That's more rigorous, but it has the opposite problem. It's often too narrow. A lot of real work isn't a clean, isolated task. It's figuring out what to build, coordinating with other people, reviewing, deciding. You can speed up one piece by a lot, and if the bottleneck is somewhere else, the overall output barely moves.

So the level I actually care about most is the end-to-end one. Are we shipping models and products faster? Are research iterations happening more quickly? Are small teams doing things that used to need large teams? That's noisier and harder to attribute cleanly, because many things change at once, but it's the thing that ultimately matters.

My honest read is that the gains are real and growing, but they show up unevenly. Where the work is mostly writing and iterating on code, the effect is large. Where the bottleneck is compute, or waiting on experiments, or human judgment about what direction to go, the tools help less, at least so far. And I think that pattern matters well beyond Anthropic. It's a bit like Amdahl's law: you speed up part of the system and the parts you didn't speed up start to dominate. So the question I keep asking isn't just "is AI making people faster," it's "what's the new bottleneck, and can the models start helping with that too?" That's where I expect the next big jump to come from.

r001.rationale: The candidate discusses the risk of mistaking individual perceptions for real productivity, but says nothing about commercial pressure to survive or retaining tools.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss competitors using Anthropic’s tools or infer a competitive advantage from that concern.

r003.rationale: It asks whether Anthropic is shipping models and products faster, but does not identify model launches as a concrete check on productivity claims.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it's harder to measure than people assume, and I'm suspicious of anyone who gives you a clean number. The thing I actually trust most is not a metric, it's what engineers do when nobody's making them do anything. If you took Claude Code away from our engineers tomorrow, there would be a revolt. That tells you something real. People don't fight to keep tools that aren't helping them.

But let me try to be more rigorous than that, because "people like it" isn't good enough. There are a few things we look at.

One is the fraction of code that's being written by the model versus by a human. Inside Anthropic, that number is now very high, well over half for a lot of teams, and in some cases most of the pull requests are substantially model-generated. Now, that by itself doesn't prove productivity. You could write a lot of bad code quickly. So you have to pair it with something like: are we shipping more? Are the things we're shipping breaking more or less often? And so far the answer is we're shipping a lot more and reliability hasn't gotten worse. That's the combination that matters.

The second thing is anecdotal but very telling, which is what people choose to do with the time. The early story of these tools was "it autocompletes your boilerplate." That's a modest gain, maybe ten or twenty percent. What we're seeing now is different in kind. Someone will say, "I had a project that I estimated at two weeks and I did it in an afternoon," or, more interestingly, "there's a thing I never would have attempted because it wasn't worth the effort, and now I just did it." That second category is where I think the real productivity lives, and it's almost invisible to conventional measurement, because you can't count tasks that previously would never have been started.

The third thing, and this is the one I think is most underappreciated, is that we're a weird company to ask this question of, because we're building the thing we're using. So there's a feedback loop. The model helps us build the next model faster, the next model is better at helping us. That's the part I pay the most attention to, because if that loop is real, it compounds, and if it compounds it's one of the most important facts about the world right now. I think it's real. I'd put it at something like: a meaningful fraction of the speedup in our research cycle is now attributable to the models themselves. Not all of it, not yet the majority, but it's not zero and it's growing.

Now, the honest caveats. We're a biased observer. We want this to be true. And there's a well-known phenomenon where people feel more productive with these tools than they measurably are, because the tool makes the work feel easier even when the total throughput hasn't changed that much. I take that seriously. So we try to look at things like calendar time to ship a feature, and we try to look at it across teams that adopted the tools at different rates. That's not a randomized trial, but it's better than vibes.

And the last thing I'd say is that the productivity gains are extremely uneven. For a very experienced engineer who knows exactly what they want, the model is a force multiplier, sometimes a huge one. For someone who doesn't yet have the judgment to know when the model is wrong, it can actually be a liability, because the code looks fine and isn't. So part of what we're learning isn't "are the tools good," it's "what does the job of an engineer become when the tools are good." That's a question we don't fully have the answer to yet, and I think most companies are a year or two behind us in even realizing they need to ask it.

r001.rationale: The response says engineers would revolt if Claude Code were removed and acknowledges that perceived productivity can exceed measured gains, but it does not connect tool retention to commercial survival pressure.

r002.rationale: It describes a model-building feedback loop, but does not discuss competitors using Anthropic’s tools or interpret that concern as evidence of competitive advantage.

r003.rationale: It cites shipping more, reliability, and feature delivery time as checks, but does not identify model launches as a concrete check.

astra-6.text:
I think you have to distinguish between people feeling more productive and the organization actually getting more done. If someone says, “This saved me three hours,” that’s useful evidence, but it’s not quite the same as showing that we’re shipping faster or doing better research.

The thing I’d want to look at is the whole loop. For engineering, how long does it take to go from deciding to build something to having it working reliably? If writing the code gets faster, but reviewing and debugging it takes longer, you haven’t necessarily gained very much. For research, it’s even harder, because generating more experiments isn’t the goal. The goal is learning something that matters.

And there’s a counterfactual problem: the tools are improving, but the people and the organization are changing at the same time. So I’d put more weight on comparisons of similar tasks with and without the tools than on a company-wide feeling that things are speeding up.

Ultimately, the strongest evidence would be that small teams can consistently accomplish things that previously required much larger teams, at the same or better quality. That’s a much more meaningful standard than how much AI-generated code there is.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes perceived productivity from organizational output, but does not say commercial survival pressure leaves little room for tools that only create an illusion of productivity.

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss competitors using Anthropic’s tools or infer a competitive advantage from that concern.

r003.rationale: It proposes measures such as delivery speed, research learning, and small-team output, but does not identify model launches as a concrete check.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you have to distinguish between people feeling more productive and the organization actually getting more done. Those can be quite different. If someone says, “This used to take me three hours, and now it takes twenty minutes,” that’s useful evidence. But you still want to know: Did the work need more review? Did we introduce bugs? And was that task actually the bottleneck?

Coding is a good example. You can generate more code without shipping useful things faster. So I’d look at the whole cycle: how quickly you go from an idea to something that works, how much human attention it takes, and what the quality is at the end.

The strongest evidence would be comparisons where otherwise similar tasks get done with and without the tools. That’s hard to do perfectly because people choose when to use them, and the tools keep changing. So I wouldn’t trust one number. I’d want several kinds of evidence pointing in the same direction—and ultimately, evidence that we’re accomplishing things we couldn’t accomplish before.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss competitors using Anthropic’s tools or infer a competitive advantage from that concern.

r003.rationale: It discusses measuring productivity through task comparisons, quality, and organizational output, but does not identify model launches as a concrete check.
